FLASHCARD SET · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Toddler Room flashcards.

Thirty-five cards that name the world a toddler actually lives in: the toys on the mat, the cup and the high chair, the crib and the night-light, the potty and the toothbrush, the shoes and the socks and the little table and chair. Every card carries an age pill and a room-area pill, so a parent can tell in one glance whether tonight is a play-time card, a sleepy-time card or a care-time card.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    Find it in the room

    Pull a card, say the word, then walk to the real thing together — the actual ball, the actual crib. Toddlers learn words by pointing at what they love, and every card is something they touch every day.

  2. 02

    Sort by the room’s areas

    Three piles: toys, mealtimes, sleep. Sorting by where things belong is a real two-year-old skill — and it tidies the actual room afterwards, which is the sneakiest bonus in this set.

  3. 03

    Name the routine, do the routine

    The care cards are routine cards: pull the toothbrush card before brushing, the soap card at the sink, the pajamas card at bedtime. The card becomes the warning that the next step is coming — and warnings prevent tantrums.

  4. 04

    Follow the age pills

    Every card shows its age pill. Start with the Ages 1+ cards as first words, then grow into the Ages 2–3 cards as routines and pretend play take off. The set grows with the child, one pill at a time.

      Ball Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Play time

      One round toy that has entertained every toddler ever born — the ball is usually the very first play word a child learns, because the game never changes: it rolls, you chase.

      Say it together

      “Ball! The ball rolls — round and round. Can you roll the ball? Roll it to me… now chase it, chase it!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sit on the floor a stride apart and roll the ball back and forth. Rolling comes before throwing, and the taking-turns rhythm is the real lesson hiding inside the game. When rolling is boring, put the ball on a sofa cushion and push it off — gravity does the comedy every time.

      Quick parent note

      Balls are the cheapest vocabulary lesson there is: one word, one toy, endless reps. Soft balls first — a toddler who gets bonked by a hard ball learns to fear the game, not love it.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Ball lesson on the Learning Path.

      Blanket Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Sleepy time

      Soft, folded and always near the crib — the blanket is the word that tells a toddler sleep is on the way, and knowing what comes next is what keeps bedtime calm.

      Say it together

      “Blanket! The soft, cozy blanket. We tuck the blanket in… cozy cozy. Night-night, blanket.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the blanket game while everyone is awake and happy: cover a teddy with the blanket — "night-night, teddy!" — then lift it — "good morning, teddy!" The toddler practises the word with a smile instead of at bedtime, and the blanket stops being a signal to fight and becomes a friend.

      Quick parent note

      Words that predict routines are tantrum insurance. Say "blanket" at the same moment you fetch it every night and the word itself becomes the wind-down — the card at the door, the calm that follows.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Blanket lesson on the Learning Path.

      Bookshelf Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Around the room

      The shelf where the books sleep between stories — the bookshelf is where a toddler learns that books have homes too, and that story time starts with choosing.

      Say it together

      “Bookshelf! The books live here, on the bookshelf. Pick a book… any book! Then it goes back on the shelf for its nap.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make the shelf the toddler’s own library: one low shelf, a few books facing covers-out. Let the child choose tonight’s story from the shelf — choosing is half of reading — and end by walking the book "home" to the shelf together. Books that get put away with ceremony get pulled out with ceremony too.

      Quick parent note

      A forward-facing bookshelf at toddler height does more for early reading than any gadget: covers invite, spines hide. The word "bookshelf" also quietly teaches the tidy-up habit every room in the house will thank you for.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Bookshelf lesson on the Learning Path.

      Bottle Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Mealtime

      The bottle is often a toddler’s very first food word — it means milk, comfort and the good feeling of a full tummy, all in one little word.

      Say it together

      “Bottle! The milk bottle. Yummy — time to drink. Hold the bottle… drink, drink. All gone!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Offer the bottle and say the word each time — bottle before milk, every time. Then let the toddler feed a doll or teddy with an empty bottle: pretending to feed is how toddlers rehearse their own mealtimes, and rehearsing makes the real thing smoother.

      Quick parent note

      Naming the bottle at every feed builds the mealtime word bank early. Many families also use the card gently when the bottle is about to retire — "bottles are for littles; big kids use cups" — a story the child has already heard a hundred times, in card form.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Bottle lesson on the Learning Path.

      Building Blocks Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Play time

      Red, yellow, green and blue — building blocks are the toddler engineering kit, and the curriculum is simple: stack it high, then knock it down with maximum drama.

      Say it together

      “Building blocks! Stack them up — one, two, three… up, up, UP! And… CRASH! Knock them down. Build it again!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Take turns adding one block to the tower — your block, their block — counting each as it lands. The turn-taking matters as much as the stacking. Then let the crash be GLORIOUS: the demolition is the reward, and blocks that are allowed to fall get built higher every time.

      Quick parent note

      Stacking is grip strength, hand-eye control and early maths wearing a game costume. And the crash is not misbehaviour — cause and effect is the most exciting physics lesson on Earth at age two.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Building Blocks lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the The Toddler Room (Extra Class) room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Changing Table Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Care time

      The flat spot where diaper changes happen — the changing table is a routine in furniture form, and naming it helps a toddler know exactly what is coming next.

      Say it together

      “Changing table! Up we go — lie down, little one. Time for a fresh diaper, then we play. All clean!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Say the word as you lift the child up and as you lay them down — the same words, every change. Toddlers fight surprises, not diaper changes. Then ask them to "hold the diaper" and hand it over: one small job turns a passive wrestle into an active job.

      Quick parent note

      A named routine is a calmer routine. The card also survives the transition: when the potty takes over, the changing table card retires gracefully — a little milestone marker in cardboard form.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Changing Table lesson on the Learning Path.

      Comb Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Care time

      The little toothed tool for tidy hair — the comb appears twice a day, every day, which makes it one of the most-practised words in the whole toddler room.

      Say it together

      “Comb! Time to comb your hair — gentle, gentle. My turn… now YOUR turn. Comb, comb, comb. All tidy!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Take turns: the grown-up combs three strokes, then the toddler combs the teddy’s fur (or your hair — enormous comedy value). Handing over the comb mid-routine gives the control-hungry toddler a share of power, which is usually the difference between a battle and a giggle.

      Quick parent note

      Hair combing is one of the first places toddlers learn that bodies have parts and routines have steps. Offering the turn — "my comb, your comb" — is cooperation training disguised as grooming.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Comb lesson on the Learning Path.

      Crayons Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Play time

      A box of five bright crayons — the first tools that make marks on purpose. Scribbling comes first, and every scribble is a masterpiece the artist will tell you all about.

      Say it together

      “Crayons! Look at the colors — red, yellow, green, blue. Scribble scribble! What did you draw? Tell me about it!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Tape a big sheet to the table and scribble side by side — one crayon each. Ask "tell me about your drawing" instead of "what is it?": at this age the story matters more than the picture. One crayon box at a time, paper always, and the dining table stays a dining table.

      Quick parent note

      Scribbling builds the grip that writing will borrow later, and being asked to narrate the scribble builds the talking that reading will borrow. The two-year-old who explains their scribble is doing pre-writing and pre-reading in one chair.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Crayons lesson on the Learning Path.

      Crib Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Sleepy time

      The bed with the bars and the yellow blanket — the crib is where sleep lives, and a toddler who can name it knows exactly what the word "crib" promises: rest is coming.

      Say it together

      “Crib! Into the crib we go. This is your bed — cozy crib, soft blanket. Night-night, sleep tight.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Use the word as the last word of the bedtime routine — the same sentence at the crib rail every night: "into the crib, night-night." Then let the toddler tuck a teddy into a doll crib or a shoebox bed first: putting the teddy to bed is the dress rehearsal for going to bed willingly.

      Quick parent note

      The crib card works because it is honest: the crib IS where the toddler sleeps, and the word said at the rail nightly becomes a cue the body answers. Toddlers who know the script fight the script less.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Crib lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the The Toddler Room (Extra Class) room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Diaper Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Care time

      The white taped thing that gets changed a dozen times a day — the diaper is the most-practised routine word in the room, and saying it out loud turns a surprise into a schedule.

      Say it together

      “Diaper! Time for a fresh diaper. Lie down, one, two… all clean! Fresh diaper, happy baby.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Narrate the change with the same short script every time — "lie down… fresh diaper… all clean!" — and hand the toddler one job: carrying the diaper to the bin, peeling the tabs, choosing front or back. One job per change keeps small hands busy and big protests small.

      Quick parent note

      Routine words are cooperation tools. The same card later moonlights as potty-training support: "diapers are for babies; the potty is for you" lands softer when the diaper has been a named, familiar friend for a year.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Diaper lesson on the Learning Path.

      Easel Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Play time

      The painting stand with the paper clipped on — the easel is where toddlers make art standing up, and standing-up scribbles build the big arm muscles small hands will need.

      Say it together

      “Easel! Stand up tall and draw — up high, down low. Clip the paper, hold the crayon… big circles on the easel!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Clip paper to any surface at standing height — the real easel, the fridge, a wall-sized box — and make big arm circles, up-down lines and loops. Standing art is different from table art: the whole shoulder works. One rule keeps it joyful: the marks live on the paper.

      Quick parent note

      Vertical scribbling is genuine pre-writing practice — the shoulder and wrist positions it builds are the ones pencil control borrows. The easel also gives high-energy toddlers a reason to be on their feet while they focus.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Easel lesson on the Learning Path.

      Floor Cushion Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Around the room

      A round blue cushion on the floor — the floor cushion is a toddler-sized spot that belongs to the toddler: a place to sit, flop, look at books and take a breath.

      Say it together

      “Floor cushion! This is YOUR soft spot. Sit on the cushion… flop! Read a book on the cushion. It is so cozy.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Park the cushion in the book corner and let it mean something: books get read HERE, cuddles happen HERE. Try the flop game — stand tall, wobble, FLOP onto the cushion with a big sigh, "aaaaah." Toddlers repeat a game with a sigh in it forever.

      Quick parent note

      A defined personal spot is quiet psychology: it gives a big-feeling toddler somewhere to retreat with dignity. The cushion also answers the toddler question "where do I fit?" with three inches of foam and a whole lot of belonging.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Floor Cushion lesson on the Learning Path.

      High Chair Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Mealtime

      The tall chair with the tray — the high chair is where meals happen, and naming it on the walk to the kitchen turns "come and sit down" into "high chair time", which toddlers accept far better.

      Say it together

      “High chair! Climb up into the high chair — up you go! The tray clicks on… time to eat. Yum yum yum.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Say the word at the same moment every meal — "high chair!" — then let the toddler climb up with a hand’s help. Give the tray one job before the food arrives: bang the spoon, put the cup in its spot. A named seat with a small ritual is a seat toddlers climb into without a wrangle.

      Quick parent note

      Mealtime battles often start before the food lands — at the climbing-in stage. The word "high chair" said cheerfully at the same point daily builds a routine the body just follows, and the card makes the word itself a fun thing to find.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the High Chair lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the The Toddler Room (Extra Class) room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Laundry Basket Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Around the room

      The woven blue basket that holds the clothes — and, between washes, holds one giggling toddler. The laundry basket is a container word, and container words are toddler gold.

      Say it together

      “Laundry basket! Put the socks IN… the towels IN… everything in the basket. And where is [child’s name]? IN the basket! Peekaboo!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the carry game: the toddler fetches one garment from the floor and drops it in the basket — "socks IN! thank you!" — one piece at a time. Then flip the game and let them climb in for a two-second peekaboo. In, out, in. The tidy-up is real and the toddler never notices.

      Quick parent note

      In-and-out is THE container schema toddlers are driven to explore, so this card meets them where they already are. The one-garment-at-a-time fetch is a genuine chore seed — the two-year-old version of laundry day.

      Teach it, step by step

      Night Light Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Sleepy time

      The little glowing lamp — the night light is the friendly face of the dark room, and it earns its place in the bedtime script the moment a toddler learns to name it.

      Say it together

      “Night light! Click… on comes the night light. The room is dark but the night light glows — soft and yellow. It watches over you all night.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make the click part of the routine: the toddler gets to flick the switch or say "night light, ON" — control over the light is control over the dark. Then say goodnight to it by name. A light the child switched on themselves guards better than one the grown-ups snuck in later.

      Quick parent note

      Fears of the dark bloom around age two, and the night light is the classic answer because it gives the child agency: they turn the dark friendly themselves. The card makes the light a named member of the bedtime team, not a crutch to be embarrassed about.

      Teach it, step by step

      Pajamas Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Sleepy time

      The soft one-piece suit with the yellow zip — pajamas are the official uniform of bedtime, and putting them on is the signal every toddler’s body learns: sleep is next.

      Say it together

      “Pajamas! Time for your sleepy clothes. Arm in… leg in… zip! Cozy pajamas mean night-night is coming.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Lay out the pajamas and name each part as it goes on — "arm in, leg in, zip!" — then let the toddler do the zip all by themselves (this is THE job; never do it for them). Zip control is fiddly, funny and disproportionately proud-making.

      Quick parent note

      The pajama word works like a countdown: clothes, then teeth, then story, then crib. Keeping the order identical nightly is what makes the card powerful — the pajamas are not clothing, they are the second hand on the bedtime clock.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Pajamas lesson on the Learning Path.

      Picture Book Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Play time

      A book with a teddy bear on the cover — the picture book is the doorway to stories, and at this age reading means pointing, naming and hearing the same favourite a hundred happy times.

      Say it together

      “Picture book! Look at the bear on the cover. Open it up… point to the pictures. What is that? A dog! And that? A ball! Read it again!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Read with a finger: your child points at pictures and you name them — the same pointing-and-naming game as this whole set, but inside a book. Repetition is the point, not variety; the tenth read of the same book is when the child starts "reading" it to you from memory.

      Quick parent note

      Point-and-name reading builds vocabulary faster than any flashcard app, because the pictures carry the meaning and the adult carries the voice. The bear on this cover is a good reminder: the best first books put ONE friendly thing on the cover and mean it.

      Teach it, step by step

      Pillow Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Sleepy time

      The blue square that waits at the head of the bed — the pillow is where the tired head lands, and "pillow" is often one of the first sleep words a toddler says.

      Say it together

      “Pillow! The soft, squishy pillow. Lay your head down… boop! Cozy pillow. Close your eyes… mmm.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the pillow flop: stand by the bed, wobble like a sleepy robot, then flop the head onto the pillow with a huge sigh — "aaaaah, pillow." Do it with a teddy first, then the toddler. The sigh is the whole game; it practises the exact muscle relaxation bedtime needs.

      Quick parent note

      Naming the pillow gives bedtime one more friendly landmark. And the flop game is genuine wind-down training: the exaggerated sigh slows the breathing, which is the same trick grown-up sleep apps charge money for.

      Teach it, step by step

      Play Mat Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Play time

      The rolled-up blue mat — the play mat is the stage the whole room plays on, and unrolling it can become the official starting whistle of playtime.

      Say it together

      “Play mat! Roll it out — tadaaa! The toys go ON the mat. Sit on the mat, play on the mat… and at tidy-up time, the toys go back and the mat rolls away.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make the mat the play boundary: toys live on the mat during play, and the roll-up is the tidy-up song’s last verse. Unrolling as the opener and rolling as the closer gives playtime a shape — beginnings and endings toddlers can see and feel.

      Quick parent note

      A defined play space quietly solves the sprawl problem: toys migrate less, tidy-up has a visible finish line, and the mat’s edge teaches "on" and "off" — two of the most useful location words in the toddler dictionary.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Play Mat lesson on the Learning Path.

      Potty Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Care time

      The little blue chair with the yellow seat — the potty is the toddler’s own toilet, and meeting the WORD long before the TRAINING makes the whole adventure less scary.

      Say it together

      “Potty! This is the potty — your very own little chair. When you are ready, pee and poo go IN the potty. Big kid stuff!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Keep the word casual and cheerful months before training starts — point at the potty, name it, let a doll or teddy "sit" on it. On training days the card becomes the script: sit, wait, "well done, you!", empty, flush. Same words every time, zero drama.

      Quick parent note

      Potty learning is mostly a language project: the child needs the words before the skills. Families who name the potty early report fewer fears around the transition — the potty is an old friend by the time it matters.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Puzzle Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Play time

      Four chunky pieces in four bright colors — the puzzle is toddler logic in wooden form: turn it, flip it, try it, CLICK, it fits. The best sound in the quiet-corner world.

      Say it together

      “Puzzle! Four pieces, four spots. Try it… turn it around… CLICK! It fits! Red in red, blue in blue. All done — do it again!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hand over ONE piece at a time instead of the whole handful — fewer choices, more wins. Narrate the trying: "turn… flip… try again… it FITS!" When a piece resists, model the calm try-again out loud; puzzles teach persistence best when the grown-up voice stays as steady as the hands.

      Quick parent note

      Puzzles are the tidy little lab of toddler thinking: matching, rotating, spatial sense and the deep life lesson that a thing that fails once can click on the next try. Four pieces is the right dose — victory without tears.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Puzzle lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Shoes Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Getting dressed

      Blue sneakers with yellow laces — shoes mean OUTSIDE, which makes this one of the most exciting words in the toddler language: shoes on means adventure on.

      Say it together

      “Shoes! Where are your shoes? There they are! Foot in… foot in… Velcro — rip! Shoes on! Ready to go outside!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sit the toddler down, present each shoe like a hat at a fancy ceremony — "one foot… other foot… rip the Velcro!" — and let them do the final rip. The Velcro job is the toddler’s contribution to getting dressed, and contributions cut dressing-time battles in half.

      Quick parent note

      The shoe word is powerful because it always predicts the same wonderful thing: going out. Naming it at the door daily builds the routine, and the foot-in-the-shoe game is the toddler’s first real dressing skill.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Shoes lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Sippy Cup Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Mealtime

      The blue cup with the green lid and two handles — the sippy cup is the bridge between bottle and open cup, and it belongs to the toddler in a way no bottle ever quite did.

      Say it together

      “Sippy cup! Here is YOUR cup. Two hands… lift… sip sip sip. Put it down. All done — good drinking!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Offer the cup at every meal with the same two-hand script, then park it in its spot when the meal ends — the cup has a home too. When the toddler masters two-hand sipping, the open-cup practice can begin with a thimble-sized splash, because the sippy cup did the heavy lifting first.

      Quick parent note

      Drinking from a cup is grip, coordination and swallowing control — a genuine skill with a genuine training arc. Naming the cup also marks ownership: MY cup, MY spot, MY job. Independence drinks from exactly this cup.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Soap Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Care time

      The pink bar by the sink — soap is the magic ingredient of clean hands, and the word works best sung: soap, bubbles, rub-a-dub, all clean.

      Say it together

      “Soap! Get the soap… water on… rub rub rub — BUBBLES! Wash the germs away. Rinse… all clean! Sparkly hands!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Wash hands together with a fixed mini-song — wet, soap, rub the fronts, rub the backs, rinse, done — and let the toddler press the soap or pump the dispenser. The bubbles are the entertainment; the routine is the lesson; the same order every time is what makes it automatic.

      Quick parent note

      Hand-washing is the first hygiene habit and the most reusable — it travels from the toddler sink to every sink for life. A named soap and a named song turn a chore into a ceremony the child runs on their own by two and a half.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Socks Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Getting dressed

      A pair of blue socks — socks are the baby step of getting dressed: stretchy, forgiving and the first garment many toddlers ever put on themselves, even if it takes a minute.

      Say it together

      “Socks! One sock… two socks. Over the toes… pull, pull, UP! Where is the other sock? THERE it is. Cozy toes!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Start the sock over the toes and let the toddler do the pulling-up — the heel-hitch can come later. Play sock hunt with the pair: one on, one missing, "where IS it?" — finding the twin is half the fun and teaches matching without a worksheet in sight.

      Quick parent note

      Pulling a sock over toes is real finger strength and real patience, celebrated early. Socks also teach the pair concept — two the same, one for each foot — which quietly seeds matching and counting long before either is taught.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Socks lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Stacking Rings Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Play time

      The rainbow stacker on its yellow post — stacking rings look like a toy and behave like a lesson: biggest at the bottom, smallest on top, and the order is the whole game.

      Say it together

      “Stacking rings! The big ring first — WHOOSH, down the pole. Then the next… and the next… and the teeny tiny one on top. All done! Rainbow tower!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hand out the rings and let the toddler discover the size rule by trial — the big ring simply will not sit on top, and the toy itself teaches sorting by size with no words needed. Then line the rings up on the floor biggest-to-smallest like a rainbow snake. Same skill, different shape.

      Quick parent note

      Ordering by size is a first maths skill and the stacker is its friendliest teacher. The toy also rewards the fail-again courage: a wrong ring can’t be forced, only rethought — which is early-years problem-solving in one wooden post.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Stacking Rings lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Stroller Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Around the room

      The blue pushchair waiting by the door — the stroller is the toddler’s own vehicle, and naming it turns the pre-walk buckle wrestle into a known routine.

      Say it together

      “Stroller! Climb into the stroller — up you go! Click the buckle… click! Wheels go round and round. Off we go!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Let the toddler climb in themselves (with a hand nearby) and do the buckle’s final click — one more small job that buys cooperation. Then hand them THEIR stroller for the dolls: pushing a teddy around the room is how toddlers rehearse both driving and being driven.

      Quick parent note

      The stroller word belongs to a routine with friction in it — leaving the park is where strollers earn their tears. A named climb-in-click ritual gives the goodbye a script, and toddlers follow scripts far better than they follow "five more minutes."

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Stuffed Bunny Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Play time

      The cream bunny with the long ears — the stuffed bunny is a toddler’s first best friend, confidant and patient student all in one soft, huggable toy.

      Say it together

      “Stuffed bunny! Soft bunny, long ears. Hug the bunny — gentle, gentle. Where are bunny’s ears? Where is bunny’s nose? Hop hop hop, little bunny!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Name the bunny’s parts — ears, nose, paws, tail — by touching each one, then ask the toddler to find them on the bunny and then on themselves: "bunny’s nose… YOUR nose!" Then bunny hops across the floor and the toddler hops too. Two-hops-and-a-hug is a complete game.

      Quick parent note

      Stuffed friends are the toddlers’ first students: everything the child is learning gets taught to the bunny, which is how the child rehearse it. The body-parts game on a beloved toy transfers to the child’s own body with almost no teaching at all.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Stuffed Bunny lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Table and Chair Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Around the room

      The small yellow table with its green and red chair — the table and chair are the toddler’s workstation, child-sized on purpose so little legs can sit flat and little arms can work.

      Say it together

      “Table and chair! Sit on the chair… scoot in… this is your table. Puzzle on the table, crayons on the table — all done? Tidy the table!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Do one activity at the table, then practise the finish: pieces back in the box, crayons in the tub, push the chair in. The push-in is the toddler’s signature on a finished job. A child-sized table also fixes posture and reach — sitting flat makes every activity easier.

      Quick parent note

      "Scoot in, push the chair in" is Montessori’s oldest move and it still works: a defined workspace with a defined finish teaches activity boundaries better than any instruction. The chair also becomes the reading chair, the snack chair and the watch-the-grown-up chair — furniture with a job.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Teddy Bear Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Play time

      The brown bear with the round tummy — the teddy bear is the classic first friend, the one that gets dragged by one arm through every meal, nap and adventure the toddler attempts.

      Say it together

      “Teddy bear! A soft brown bear. Hug your teddy — squeeze! Feed the teddy, walk the teddy… and at night, teddy sleeps in the crib too. Night-night, teddy.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Let the teddy join everything: he "eats" a spoonful, he gets his teeth brushed (own toothbrush, no paste), he sits on the potty, he goes to bed first. The toddler who parents a teddy is rehearsing every routine in this set — and rehearsed routines run smoother when it is the toddler’s turn.

      Quick parent note

      A teddy is both a comfort object and a rehearsal stage: whatever the child does with the bear is what the child is learning to do themselves. Big feelings also talk to bears more easily than to grown-ups, which makes the teddy the cheapest therapist in the room.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Toothbrush Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 2–3Care time

      The blue brush with the yellow stripe — the toothbrush comes out twice a day for life, which makes the toddler years the perfect time to make it a friendly, named routine.

      Say it together

      “Toothbrush! Time to brush the teeth — round and round, round and round. Front teeth, back teeth… spit! All clean. Sparkly smile!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Let the toddler brush first (munching the bristles is normal), then the grown-up finishes the job — the "you, then me" handover keeps both cooperation and cleanliness. Sing the same four-line brush song every time; when the song is the timer, nobody watches the clock.

      Quick parent note

      Brushing is a lifetime habit installed in the bathroom of the toddler years. The word, the song and the two-step handover are what make it stick — and a teddy with his own brush doubles the enthusiasm for free.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Towel Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Care time

      The folded blue towel — the towel is the grand finale of every bath: wrapped up warm, dried head to toe and popped out the other side a clean, cozy toddler.

      Say it together

      “Towel! Time to get dry — wrap you up like a burrito! Rub the head… rub the toes… all dry! Cozy and warm.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Dry in the same order every bath — head, tummy, toes — naming each part as the towel finds it: "towel dries the HEAD… towel dries the TOES." Then let the toddler dry a doll the same way. The named order teaches body parts and makes the end of bath time predictable.

      Quick parent note

      The towel is also the toddler’s first laundry helper: by two they can hold a corner, and by three they can spread it flat. Every routine word in this set doubles as a job, and jobs are how toddlers join the family team.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Toy Car Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Play time

      The little red car with blue wheels — the toy car is often the first toy a toddler pushes, and pushing a car is how a first story begins: it goes somewhere, it comes back, it goes fast.

      Say it together

      “Toy car! Vroom vroom — the car drives! Push it… round the rug… UP the cushion and down — wheee! Stop at the light… go! Vroom vroom.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Build a ramp from a sofa cushion and let the car fly, then park it in a shoebox "garage". Add the traffic words — stop, go, fast, slow — and the game quietly becomes vocabulary practice. Two cars means one for you, one for me: the toddler’s first shared race.

      Quick parent note

      Pushing cars builds finger strength and aim, and the stop-go game plants the traffic words every ride will use. Cars also carry the first little stories — where is the car going? to Grandma’s! — which is pretend play pulling out of the driveway.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Toy Drum Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Play time

      The red drum with the yellow rims and two sticks — the toy drum is the loudest friend in the room and the toddler’s first instrument: every bang is a beat, and beats are music.

      Say it together

      “Toy drum! Bang bang BANG! Loud! Now softly, softly… quiet taps. Fast beats… slow beats… and… STOP. Hands up!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Copy-cat drumming: you play loud, the toddler plays loud; you tap soft, they tap soft; you speed up, they speed up. The loud-soft-fast-slow game is the whole first music curriculum. Then the drum sleeps in a cupboard corner — the stop rule is part of the game, said with a smile.

      Quick parent note

      Drumming teaches listening as much as banging: copying a rhythm is attention training with sticks. The loud-soft contrast also seeds the "inside voice" idea — the drum’s quiet mode is where inside voices are born.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Toy Drum lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

      Toy Train Flashcard for Toddlers

      Ages 1+Play time

      The green engine with the red trim and two little carriages — the toy train runs on rug tracks and toddler imagination, and every chuff-chuff is a chance to say the words with it.

      Say it together

      “Toy train! Choo choo! The train goes chuff chuff chuff… round the rug… under the table… STOP at the station. All aboard! Choo choo!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Lay a figure-eight track or just run the train round the rug, and build the journey with words — over the cushion mountain, through the chair tunnel, stop at the station. Take turns being the driver. The toddler adds the choo-choo; you add the stops; the story grows one lap at a time.

      Quick parent note

      Trains carry two of a toddler’s favourite things at once: wheels that go and a line that connects — engine, carriage, carriage. That connecting idea (and the stop-and-go words) make the toy train a vocabulary engine that keeps pulling new words behind it.

      Teach it, step by step
